title: Artie and Angie and Hank and Hercules

jokes.text: Artie delivers a high-minded speech about discipline and professionalism, then immediately asks his assistant to fetch him a roll-up sweater
jokes.setup: Artie opens with a sermon about discipline, sustained professionalism, and focus being essential to quality television
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to asking about sweater colors, exposing his speech as self-serving hot air
jokes.explanation: The cold open is a perfectly structured ironic bait-and-switch. The lofty language ('sustained level of professionalism') collapses the moment Artie pivots to consumer shopping. It's quintessentially Artie — the man who can project authority while doing absolutely nothing consequential. The joke is in the gap between the rhetoric and the reality, which is the show's entire thesis.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If you're gonna sit around all day with your thumb up your ass, sooner or later that will impact the show.

jokes.text: "I hate when people use their children as an excuse."
jokes.setup: Mary Lou reports that Sigourney Weaver has canceled because her child is sick
jokes.punchline: Artie responds with naked contempt for the idea that sick children are a legitimate reason to cancel
jokes.explanation: Short, brutal, perfectly in character. Artie's worldview — the show is everything — is crystallized in five words. The economy here is excellent; the joke does its work immediately and without elaboration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I hate when people use their children as an excuse.

jokes.text: "Mary Lou, that's the reason people in Hollywood have kids."
jokes.setup: Artie explains to the new assistant why he hates the sick-child cancellation excuse
jokes.punchline: He reveals his cynical insider belief that Hollywood people have children specifically to use as excuses
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely sharp piece of Hollywood satire. It's cynical, specific, and rings with insider truth. Artie delivers it as mentorship, which makes it darker and funnier. The line works because it's almost plausible as showbiz wisdom. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Mary Lou, that's the reason people in Hollywood have kids.

jokes.text: Artie scolds Mary Lou for discussing the cancellation in front of Larry — while Larry is clearly present and engaged in sweater shopping, completely oblivious
jokes.setup: Artie reprimands Mary Lou for upsetting Larry with the cancellation news
jokes.punchline: Larry is visibly unbothered, focused on sweaters — Artie's protective instinct is completely misread and unnecessary
jokes.explanation: A nice visual irony — Artie's whole speech about protecting Larry from upsetting news is undercut by Larry cheerfully ignoring it all in favor of a woodland jacket. The joke lives in the staging more than the dialogue, which is classic Larry Sanders Show.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Boy, I'd like to have that police woman put me in a choke hold. You know, frisk me, baby. Whoa, do I have a concealed weapon for you.

jokes.text: Hank's escalating Angie Dickinson fantasy monologue: "Boy, I'd like to have that police woman put me in a choke hold. You know, frisk me, baby. Whoa, do I have a concealed weapon for you."
jokes.setup: The room has just heard Angie Dickinson will be a guest
jokes.punchline: Hank launches into an increasingly sleazy sexual fantasy riff on the Policewoman character, culminating in 'concealed weapon'
jokes.explanation: The joke is almost entirely carried by Hank's character — the creepily enthusiastic, aging lech who never reads the room. The wordplay ('concealed weapon') is adequate but not sharp. Works because Tambor makes Hank's lack of self-awareness so complete.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Shut up, Hank. Officer, officer, turn off that siren and let's fuck.

jokes.text: "Shut up, Hank. Officer, officer, turn off that siren and let's fuck."
jokes.setup: Hank is mid-fantasy riff about Angie Dickinson's Policewoman character
jokes.punchline: Artie, who has his own history with Angie, can't help but top Hank's riff with a blunter, raunchier version — revealing his own investment
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the raw vulgarity of the line itself, and the character reveal — Artie shuts down Hank while immediately doing the same thing, worse. The economy is excellent: 'turn off that siren and let's fuck' is maximally efficient. Character integration is high because this is distinctly Artie's voice.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're gonna have to be more specific.

jokes.text: "You're gonna have to be more specific."
jokes.setup: Artie asks Larry if he's ever had a woman who scrambled his brains and made him think with his dick
jokes.punchline: Larry, a chronic womanizer, deadpans that Artie will need to narrow it down
jokes.explanation: Textbook economy and character integration. Four words that tell you everything about Larry Sanders — vain, self-aware about his own weakness, slightly proud of it. The structure is perfect: Artie's question is long and earnest, making Larry's brevity land harder. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, we had a lot of hot sex, but we never left the house.

jokes.text: "She's like a siren calling for me to smash my nuts upon the rocks."
jokes.setup: Artie is explaining the power Angie has over him using the classical siren metaphor
jokes.punchline: The metaphor pivots from poetic ('smash upon the rocks') to crudely anatomical ('smash my nuts')
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout lines. It earns its laugh through the collision of elevated literary reference (the Odyssey's sirens) with blunt vulgarity. The surprise is in how late the punchline word arrives — you're already in the classical metaphor before 'nuts' lands. Highly quotable, distinctly Artie's voice — no other character on television speaks like this.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: She's like a siren calling for me to smash my nuts upon the rocks.

jokes.text: "She's like, uh, booze to me. The only difference with angie is I... [cut] I don't know when to stop. Ha! OK, it's not that different."
jokes.setup: Artie starts to explain Angie is like booze — there's a difference — then cuts to him saying 'I don't know when to stop'
jokes.punchline: He immediately realizes the metaphor collapsed: he doesn't know when to stop with booze either. 'It's not that different.'
jokes.explanation: The scene cut is used as the structural device — the joke is that the cut represents Artie's pause to think, and when we return he's realized his analogy is self-defeating. This is sophisticated structural comedy: the edit IS the punchline. The self-correction ('OK, it's not that different') is delivered with perfect Artie equanimity. Strong craft score because the joke requires both good writing and good editing to land.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Ha! OK, it's not that different.

jokes.text: Hank's assistant Brian and writer Phil mob Don Rickles in the greenroom begging him to insult them
jokes.setup: Brian and Phil encounter the real Don Rickles in the greenroom and are starstruck
jokes.punchline: They begin pathetically begging him to insult them — his famous act — like fans demanding an autograph
jokes.explanation: A clever showbiz meta-joke: Rickles is famous for insults, so fans ask for insults the way they'd ask for a signature. The cringe of their desperation ('just a little one,' 'call me a hockey puck') escalates nicely. The premise is original and the scene plays on Rickles's real-life persona.

dialogue.line: Hey, could you insult us?

jokes.text: Rickles insults Brian: "You must have come out of your mother on an angle and hit the wall. You got a funny-looking body."
jokes.setup: Brian begs Rickles to insult him 'both barrels'
jokes.punchline: Rickles delivers a specific physical insult about Brian's birth and body shape
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny — the 'came out on an angle and hit the wall' image is vivid and specific enough to elevate it above generic insult comedy. The joke is aided enormously by Rickles's real persona and delivery. Would score lower if said by a fictional character.

dialogue.speaker: Don Rickles
dialogue.line: Oh, not really, you know, I don't do that. You know, I do that for, you know, when you get paid.

jokes.text: "Are you a queer? / No. / Hey, you're not in the life. Not the last time I checked. / I'll do the funny stuff. Shut up."
jokes.setup: Rickles asks Brian if he's gay after his 'cadet suit' insult; Brian denies it
jokes.punchline: Brian's attempt to participate in the riff ('not the last time I checked') is shut down by Rickles — 'I'll do the funny stuff'
jokes.explanation: The meta-punchline ('I'll do the funny stuff. Shut up.') is the real joke here and it's sharp — Rickles asserting professional hierarchy while mid-insult session is perfectly in character and also a comment on the dynamics of comedy performance. Works on multiple levels.

dialogue.speaker: Don Rickles
dialogue.line: You must have come out of your mother on an angle and hit the wall. You got a funny-looking body.

jokes.text: "There he is! Mr. Warm!" — Hank's greeting to Don Rickles
jokes.setup: Hank arrives in the greenroom after Rickles has just finished brutally insulting two people
jokes.punchline: Hank's sycophantic nickname for Rickles — 'Mr. Warm' — is perfectly ironic given what just happened
jokes.explanation: A tight, economical ironic joke. 'Mr. Warm' as a nickname for Rickles — the most famous insulter in show business — is a sharp bit of irony that requires no elaboration. Hank's oblivious enthusiasm makes it land better.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It's like I shit in Pluto's dish or something.

jokes.text: Hank asks Rickles to get him in at Disney: "I can't get my foot in the door at disney. It's like I shit in pluto's dish or something."
jokes.setup: Hank wants Rickles (who voiced a character in Toy Story) to help him get a Disney job
jokes.punchline: Hank's metaphor for his Disney rejection — having defecated in Pluto the dog's food bowl — is absurdly specific and vividly lowbrow
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Shit in Pluto's dish' is absurdly specific — why Pluto? The specificity of the Disney character chosen (a dog, who has a dish) makes the image vividly gross and funny. Only Hank would reach for this metaphor while simultaneously asking a favor. The character integration is high: this is Hank's desperate, self-sabotaging social manner exactly.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I knew television was in deep, deep trouble the day they took C.P.O. Sharkey off the air.

jokes.text: Hank reminisces about C.P.O. Sharkey being canceled as a tragedy for television
jokes.setup: Hank is supposedly asking Rickles for a favor but pivots to discussing their shared bond over Rickles's old TV show
jokes.punchline: C.P.O. Sharkey was a moderately received late-70s sitcom — Hank's declaration that TV was in 'deep, deep trouble' the day it was canceled is absurd hyperbole that reveals his shallow showbiz sentimentality
jokes.explanation: A nice piece of showbiz insider comedy — the joke requires knowing (or intuiting) that C.P.O. Sharkey was not a landmark of television history. Hank's breathless sincerity makes it work. Slightly bloated in execution — the scene trails off without a clean button.

dialogue.speaker: Don Rickles
dialogue.line: What am I, with the Mossad? I don't know.

jokes.text: "What is that word you used that refers to someone who's asking for too much? What is it? It's called a chazzer." / "What am I, with the mossad? I don't know."
jokes.setup: Larry asks Rickles on-air to define the Yiddish word 'chazzer' he heard during the commercial break
jokes.punchline: Rickles deflects with 'What am I, with the Mossad?' — an absurdist refusal to be a cultural authority delivered with mock paranoia
jokes.explanation: The Mossad non sequitur is genuinely funny — Rickles treating a request to define a Yiddish word as if it's an intelligence demand. The joke works because of the absurd leap in the response. 'What am I, with the Mossad' is quotable on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Don Rickles
dialogue.line: Here's a man that's a nebbish. That means, as you can see, does nothing, just sits there and smells his hand.

jokes.text: "Well, when it's a Jew hour, we'll talk about chazzer."
jokes.setup: Larry presses Rickles to explain 'chazzer' on air
jokes.punchline: Rickles promises to address Jewish vocabulary only during a dedicated programming block
jokes.explanation: Short and pointed. 'Jew hour' as a mock programming concept is Rickles at his best — owning his identity while making it absurd. The economy is excellent: the joke takes five words. Distinctly in Rickles's voice.

dialogue.speaker: Angie
dialogue.line: Artie, forget about it, huh? You're old. It's over. Go out to the cemetery and pick out a plot.

jokes.text: "Here's a man that's a nebbish... that means, as you can see, does nothing, just sits there and smells his hand."
jokes.setup: Rickles is now defining 'nebbish' by pointing to someone on set
jokes.punchline: His definition of nebbish includes the specific detail of 'smells his hand' — adding a disgusting visual specificity to an otherwise standard definition
jokes.explanation: The 'smells his hand' detail is the joke — it's unexpected and grotesque, taking the definition from abstract to vividly specific. Rickles's delivery of practical definitions as insults is his signature and it works well here.

jokes.text: "Are you kidding? I wouldn't miss it. Have you seen how that woman looks? Are you crazy?" — Rickles on staying for Angie Dickinson
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Rickles wants to stay for Angie Dickinson's appearance
jokes.punchline: Rickles's enthusiasm is so emphatic it becomes comic — three separate exclamation-points of disbelief that anyone would even ask
jokes.explanation: Functional laugh from Rickles's comic energy but not particularly crafted. The joke is in the delivery, not the writing. Works as a scene-ender.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He's just thanking her for doing the show.

jokes.text: Angie flirts outrageously with Artie on Larry's show — 'do you know that your producer is a very sexy man?'
jokes.setup: Larry has called Artie out from behind the scenes to appear on camera to answer a timing question
jokes.punchline: Angie immediately redirects the segment to gush about Artie's sexiness in front of the live audience and Larry
jokes.explanation: The joke is structural: Larry has spent the whole episode trying to manage the Artie/Angie dynamic, and the moment Artie appears on set Angie immediately blows up the interview. The payoff of Artie's earlier request ('don't leave me alone with her') is delivered in public, on Larry's own show. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, no. Not really. Uh, he'd been on the plane the flight before mine. You could still feel the Eisner in the air.

jokes.text: "Why don't we hose these two down before they're out of control?"
jokes.setup: Angie and Artie are flirting obviously on Larry's show during Larry's interview
jokes.punchline: Larry deadpans an animal-control metaphor for his own guests
jokes.explanation: A sharp Larry line — the 'hose them down' image is vivid and the deadpan delivery suits his character perfectly. He's trying to maintain show-host composure while clearly irritated, which is the Larry Sanders sweet spot.

dialogue.speaker: Disney Executive
dialogue.line: That's Samson.

jokes.text: "Forget about it, huh? You're old. It's over. Go out to the cemetery and pick out a plot."
jokes.setup: Angie continues fawning over Artie; Larry is trying to regain control of his own interview segment
jokes.punchline: Larry tells Artie to give up on love and go pre-select his burial plot
jokes.explanation: A genuinely dark and funny line. 'Go out to the cemetery and pick out a plot' is specific enough to be vivid and dark enough to shock slightly. The context — Larry is being somewhat jealous and petty, not actually concerned about Artie's mortality — adds a layer. Strong character work: Larry's passive-aggression toward Artie is a show staple.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I don't think so.

jokes.text: "Don't pick on him. He's really sexy." / "Oh, well, it's a matter of taste." / "I never embraced him. I have my girl."
jokes.setup: Larry tells Artie to give up and pick a cemetery plot; Angie defends Artie's sexiness
jokes.punchline: Artie deflects by claiming fidelity to 'my girl' — presumably Angie herself — while being diplomatically evasive about their history in front of the live audience
jokes.explanation: The comedy of Artie claiming fidelity to the woman he's about to ditch to Italy with is a light irony that mostly sets up later payoffs. Works as connective tissue rather than a strong standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Is he a gynecologist?

jokes.text: Artie ambushes Larry from behind and kisses him on the back of the head, mistaking him for Angie
jokes.setup: Artie has clearly been unable to restrain himself and has come looking for Angie in her dressing room
jokes.punchline: He plants a kiss on the back of Larry's head, realizing too late it's not Angie — followed by an extended awkward apology
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy here is the episode's most viscerally funny moment — Artie's self-control has completely collapsed, and the tableau of him kissing Larry while both Angie and Larry react is rich. The callback context (Artie promised to stay away) makes it land harder. The extended mumbled apology ('forgive me, please forgive me') escalates the cringe. Strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It's fine. I'm that way when Siegfried and Roy are on.

jokes.text: Beverly's non-reaction to the chaos: "He's just thanking her for doing the show." — delivered over what is clearly a much more chaotic scene
jokes.setup: The dressing room scene has descended into Artie kissing Larry and passionately pursuing Angie
jokes.punchline: Beverly's completely flat gloss on the situation to nobody in particular
jokes.explanation: A perfectly economical line. Beverly's complete removal from the emotional reality of what's happening — reducing Artie's passion to a standard post-show pleasantry — is very funny. Eight words that get the full laugh. Classic Larry Sanders Show supporting character work.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Tomorrow let's switch to beer.

jokes.text: Hank at the Disney audition: "No, no. Not really. Uh, he'd been on the plane the flight before mine. You could still feel the eisner in the air."
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to impress the Disney executives by claiming a connection to Michael Eisner — 'I once sat next to Michael Eisner on a plane'
jokes.punchline: He immediately retracts — Eisner was on a previous flight — but insists the 'feeling' of Eisner still lingered in the cabin
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. The structure is a three-beat compression of Hank's entire character arc: brag, deflate, then desperately salvage with 'you could still feel the Eisner in the air.' The absurdist pivot — claiming psychic residue of a celebrity in plane air — is completely specific to Hank, who would never recognize how pathetic this sounds. It's also a brilliant satire of showbiz name-dropping culture. The joke requires no explanation and would make a room of comedy writers laugh out loud. Quotability is 9: this line travels.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You know who's really good in this one? David Schwimmer. He's hilarious in this one.

jokes.text: Hank suggests Hercules let his hair grow out — and when corrected that it's Samson, says 'I don't think so.'
jokes.setup: Hank is preparing to audition for Hercules and muses that maybe he should have let his hair grow out like Hercules did when 'they cut it and he was weak'
jokes.punchline: The executive corrects him — that's Samson, not Hercules — and Hank simply replies 'I don't think so,' refusing to accept the correction
jokes.explanation: Four words — 'I don't think so' — that encapsulate Hank's entire character. He's auditioning for a role and doesn't know basic mythology about it, and when corrected he doubles down rather than accept the embarrassment. The confidence of ignorance. The pause before 'I don't think so' is doing enormous work. This is expert character comedy: only Hank Kingsley, as written, would respond this way.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, boy, he's just like Marcel Marceau.

jokes.text: "Is he a gynecologist? That's very good. Thank you." — Hank's joke about Hercules' '12 labors'
jokes.setup: The Disney executive explains this is the scene where Hercules sets out to perform the first of his 12 labors
jokes.punchline: Hank riffs that 'labors' sounds like obstetrics and asks if Hercules is a gynecologist, then compliments his own joke
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Hank complimenting his own mediocre pun — 'That's very good. Thank you.' — because it's exactly the behavior of someone who doesn't realize they're bombing an audition. The wordplay itself is weak but the self-congratulation is the real punch. Works because of character context.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Not on TV.

jokes.text: "Do I get the part? Joking, joking." — Hank at the Disney audition
jokes.setup: The Disney exec asks if Hank has any questions before his audition
jokes.punchline: Hank jokes that he wants to know if he gets the part, then has to immediately walk it back — revealing his actual desperation
jokes.explanation: The 'joking, joking' retreat is more revealing than the joke itself — Hank is trying to defuse his own neediness. Competently executed cringe but not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If Dressed to Kill were on right now, you'd be humping the set crying out 'Mama mia!'

jokes.text: "Let's get ready to rumble!" — Hank's pre-audition declaration
jokes.setup: Hank is about to read for the Hercules audition
jokes.punchline: Instead of preparing professionally, Hank adopts a boxing announcer catchphrase — revealing his confusion about the nature of the event
jokes.explanation: Mild cringe laugh. The catchphrase is too familiar to be original but works as character illustration — Hank confusing an audition with an athletic event tells us everything. The awkward silence that presumably follows is funnier than the line itself.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What are they doing, a live action version of Dumbo? You throw in 40 pounds, a little gray makeup, you're gonna be great.

jokes.text: Hank's Hercules audition line about 'Greia the Magpie and Tivius the Beaver' — clearly invented, non-canonical animal sidekicks
jokes.setup: Hank is reading the Hercules script, which mentions helping friends defeat a lion
jokes.punchline: Hank's version of the script suddenly introduces 'Greia the magpie and Tivius the Beaver' — either improvised or from a completely different version of the script he's invented
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of Hank apparently going off-script with completely invented animal companions is wonderfully Hank — either he hasn't read the actual script or he's 'improving' it. 'Tivius the Beaver' specifically is a great comic detail. The executives' silence is the real punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What are they doing, a live action version of Dumbo? You throw in 40 pounds, a little gray makeup, you're gonna be great.

jokes.text: Hank's Hercules speech ending with 'my new friends Greia the Magpie and Tivius the Beaver'
jokes.setup: Hank is performing the Hercules speech with genuine commitment and growing confidence
jokes.punchline: The speech ends with invented Disney-style animal sidekick names ('Tivius the Beaver') that don't exist in Greek mythology, apparently written into the script
jokes.explanation: The joke is a comment on how Disney Disneyifies classical mythology — the real Hercules myth gets cute animal sidekicks like Tivius the Beaver grafted onto it. Hank delivers it with full sincerity, making the absurdity land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: This is a warning, my friend. You do not mess with Hercules. I killed my wife, I killed my children, and I shall kill you if you do not temper thy tongue.

jokes.text: "It's fine. I'm that way when siegfried and Roy are on."
jokes.setup: Larry apologizes for rushing Artie out of Angie's dressing room; Artie says it's fine
jokes.punchline: Artie reveals he behaves the same way around the famous Las Vegas magician-and-tiger duo — implying Artie has a pattern of being sidelined when Larry's desires conflict with his own
jokes.explanation: The Siegfried and Roy reference is unexpected and specific, which is what makes it funny. The implication — that there's a whole catalog of times Larry has pushed Artie aside for his own whims — is delivered with complete Artie equanimity. The specificity of the celebrity choice elevates a standard 'it's fine' beat.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I don't mean to question your judgment, but one of my balls is as big as Tate Donovan.

jokes.text: Larry walks in on Artie at his home late at night with Laura Leighton (a Melrose Place actress), not knowing she'd be there — and Artie is clearly watching Melrose Place
jokes.setup: Larry arrives at Artie's home late to apologize; he doesn't know Artie has company
jokes.punchline: The company turns out to be a recognizable Melrose Place actress — a show the episode has already established Larry finds ridiculous — in a visually ironic tableau
jokes.explanation: The visual joke of Artie — the gruff, old-school TV professional — watching Melrose Place with one of its stars is delightfully absurd. The cringe of Larry's interruption is well-executed. Works on multiple levels as a sight gag that also deepens character.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hiageus, the village idiot, enters, a sad little stump of a man with a sorry mustache. He's being pelted with stones by a band of toughs. He cries out for Hercules in his funny squeal of a voice.

jokes.text: "Oh! Melrose place. Hey, you're wonderful. I watch it. I'm just hooked."
jokes.setup: Artie is introduced to Laura Leighton from Melrose Place
jokes.punchline: Artie — the hardboiled TV veteran — immediately reveals he's an enthusiastic, hooked Melrose Place viewer
jokes.explanation: The character reversal is the joke — Artie, who projects pure Old Hollywood taste, is secretly addicted to a primetime soap. 'I'm just hooked' delivered with Rip Torn's flat candor is very funny. The joke pays off later when the Venice scenes reveal his Melrose obsession runs even deeper.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Do you think that when Hiageus gets in trouble, he could say, uh, 'Hey, now!'

jokes.text: "Yeah, we're not on... we're not on the show now." — Laura Leighton clarifying she's not currently on Melrose Place, presumably in response to Artie's fandom
jokes.setup: Artie gushes about Melrose Place; the actress apparently has to clarify her current status on the show
jokes.punchline: An awkward beat where a famous person has to explain to a fan that their fandom may be outdated
jokes.explanation: A mild awkward beat that plays on the cringe of celebrity encounters. Not especially crafted but contributes to the scene's comedic texture.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: And is that your tail I see between your legs?

jokes.text: Artie: 'Italy. Angie's got a villa in Venice and she asked me to stay with her there and I gotta go. I just can't help myself.'
jokes.setup: Artie came to apologize to Larry for the dressing room incident and say good-bye.
jokes.punchline: He's leaving for Italy with Angie — the very scenario he asked Larry to help him avoid. The promise has lasted approximately three hours.
jokes.explanation: The full callback payoff to the 'keep me away from her' plot. Artie — who managed the situation with complete authority — has completely surrendered to his impulses. The gap between his self-image as the steady hand and his actual behavior is the episode's central comic truth.

dialogue.speaker: Laura
dialogue.line: I'm just not sure that I'm ready to be in a relationship with someone in show business.
Exactly.

jokes.text: Artie announces he's going to Italy with Angie and asks Larry if he understands — using his new relationship with Laura Leighton as the moral framework
jokes.setup: Artie tells Larry he's abandoning the show to go to Angie's Venice villa and asks him to understand because 'I'm crazy about her'
jokes.punchline: The 'her' in Artie's speech refers to Angie — but he cites Larry's relationship with Laura Leighton as evidence Larry should understand romantic irresistibility, while himself abandoning the show for a completely different woman
jokes.explanation: The irony is structural: Artie invokes Larry's new relationship as justification for a choice that undermines it. Works as character comedy — Artie's self-justifying logic is hilariously shameless. The 'roughly how long?' exchange sharpens the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: We were on vacation, for Christ's sake. You know, it started out good, but then she wanted to talk about my peccadilloes. My mood swings, my temper, my stubbornness. My obsession with Glenlivet.

jokes.text: "Roughly how long would you be going?" / "Oh, just 3 days." / "OK" [as if that's somehow acceptable]
jokes.setup: Artie announces he's leaving immediately for Venice with Angie, abandoning the show
jokes.punchline: Larry's practical question ('roughly how long') and Artie's breezy 'just 3 days' — as if deserting your job mid-week for a romantic escapade is a minor scheduling matter
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in how quickly both men normalize the situation — Artie reduces it to an innocuous time question and Larry accepts the framing. 'Just 3 days' delivered with complete lightness is the punchline. The whole exchange is very Larry Sanders — catastrophes are handled as minor inconveniences.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What time's your flight?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: 9:30. I'll be back on Monday. I swear.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Thanks, buddy.

jokes.text: "Ciao. Ciao, padrio." — Artie's parting words as he heads to Italy
jokes.setup: Artie is leaving for Venice with Angie
jokes.punchline: His attempt at Italian — 'ciao, padrio' (not a real phrase) — delivered with complete confidence by a man who absolutely does not speak Italian
jokes.explanation: A small joke — Artie's confident, incorrect Italian. 'Padrio' isn't Italian, which makes the confidence funnier. Works as a button on the scene.

jokes.text: "What is it you found, exactly?" — Larry's parting question to Artie
jokes.setup: Artie has told Larry he 'hopes Larry finds what he found' as he leaves for Venice
jokes.punchline: Larry's sincere and slightly baffled follow-up question reveals he has genuinely no idea what Artie means, and neither does the audience fully
jokes.explanation: The question lands because it punctures Artie's romantic grandeur. Artie has just delivered a big parting speech and Larry's response is genuine confusion about what he means. Perfect Larry energy — the show-host who can't afford to be swept up in sentiment.

jokes.text: "Well, I'm afraid we're getting in a little bit of a rut, sweetie. All we've done since we got here is drink wine and screw."
jokes.setup: The Venice honeymoon with Angie seems to be going perfectly
jokes.punchline: Artie's complaint about their Venice trip — drinking wine and having sex — delivered as if describing a tedious domestic routine
jokes.explanation: A beautifully crafted inversion joke. Artie frames a fantasy romantic scenario as a boring rut — 'all we've done is drink wine and screw' — with the word 'afraid' doing enormous work. The deadpan complaint about paradise is very Artie, and it's perfectly economical. High craft: the joke earns its laugh through character specificity and structural inversion, not cheap shock.

jokes.text: "What do you suggest?" / "Tomorrow let's switch to beer."
jokes.setup: Angie asks what they should do differently since Artie has declared their wine-and-sex routine a 'rut'
jokes.punchline: Artie's solution to the 'rut' is to substitute wine with beer — not to change the core activities at all
jokes.explanation: The episode's second-best joke, and by craft metrics arguably the tightest. The setup beautifully positions a follow-up question expecting a romantic resolution. The punchline — 'switch to beer' — is the most economical possible subversion: four words that reveal Artie has no interest in changing anything except the specific beverage. The misdirection is perfect. The joke rewards smart comedy viewers. Very high quotability.

jokes.text: Artie admits he was distracted after the shower because he was 'a little worried about Larry' — in the middle of a romantic Italian getaway
jokes.setup: Angie notices Artie seemed distracted when he got out of the shower
jokes.punchline: Artie reveals he was thinking about his boss/star during what should be an intimate moment — his co-dependence with Larry intrudes even into Venice
jokes.explanation: The character integration here is nearly perfect — Artie's bond with Larry is revealed as more consuming than any romantic relationship he could have. The comedy is that he's completely earnest about this, with no self-awareness that it's strange. 'Not without me he isn't' is the key line: Artie defines himself through Larry, which is simultaneously touching and absurd.

jokes.text: "Not without me he isn't." — Artie on whether Larry is fine without him
jokes.setup: Angie reassures Artie that Larry is fine without him
jokes.punchline: Artie flatly, completely sincerely disagrees — 'Not without me he isn't'
jokes.explanation: Five words. Artie's complete, unironic certainty that Larry cannot function without him — delivered mid-romantic-vacation — is both funny and strangely poignant. The character integration is exceptional: this is exactly Artie's brand of protective arrogance about his role. The economy is nearly perfect. Among the best character lines in the episode.

jokes.text: "Can we turn that off?" — Larry asking to turn off Melrose Place while watching it with Laura Leighton in parallel with Artie watching it in Venice
jokes.setup: Larry and his new girlfriend Laura Leighton (a Melrose Place actress) are watching TV together
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately wants to turn off Melrose Place — rejecting it even while watching with one of its stars, which parallels Artie being obsessed with it
jokes.explanation: The intercutting between Larry dismissing Melrose and Artie obsessively watching it in Venice is a structural joke that works across scenes. Larry's dismissiveness in front of its star is also cringe-funny. Works better as part of the parallel structure than as a standalone moment.

jokes.text: Laura's deadpan response to Larry's David Schwimmer claim: 'Very fucking funny.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just claimed David Schwimmer is 'hilarious' in Melrose Place.
jokes.punchline: Laura's flat, profane dismissal.
jokes.explanation: Perfect straight-man response. Works in the context of the scene.

jokes.text: "David schwimmer. He's hilarious in this one. Very fucking funny." — Larry attributing his Melrose Place viewing to David Schwimmer
jokes.setup: Larry claims he's seen Melrose Place and that it's good — he's watching it with one of its stars
jokes.punchline: He attributes the show's appeal to David Schwimmer, who is not in Melrose Place (he's from Friends) — and says it with complete conviction
jokes.explanation: A sharp, layered joke. Larry is clearly lying about having watched Melrose Place (to seem culturally current in front of its star), and his evidence — citing David Schwimmer, who is definitively not in Melrose Place — exposes the lie hilariously. 'Very fucking funny' delivered with false conviction is the cherry on top. Works both as celebrity-name comedy and as character-specific self-deception.

jokes.text: "And do what?" / "You read my mind." — Larry and Laura's shorthand for staying in and having sex
jokes.setup: Laura says she wants to stay in tonight
jokes.punchline: Larry responds 'you read my mind' — a quick implied-sex joke that's more charming than clever
jokes.explanation: A functional but unoriginal exchange. The parallel to Artie's Venice situation is the only interesting thing about it — two couples simultaneously choosing intimacy over activity. The joke itself is thin.

jokes.text: Artie watching Italian-dubbed Larry Sanders and laughing: "Larry's a killer in any language."
jokes.setup: Artie has found a rerun of Larry Sanders on Italian TV and is watching it over Angie's objections
jokes.punchline: Artie declares Larry transcends the language barrier — even though the whole point of dubbing is that the jokes don't translate
jokes.explanation: A beautifully absurd expression of Artie's devotion to Larry. That he would watch Italian-dubbed episodes of his own show while on a romantic vacation in Venice — and declare it superior viewing — is peak Artie. 'Like Marcel Marceau' is also a great beat: Angie is acknowledging the show works visually, which isn't quite the compliment Artie takes it as.

jokes.text: "Oh, boy, he's just like Marcel Marceau. Larry's a killer in any language."
jokes.setup: Angie watches the Italian-dubbed Larry Sanders with Artie
jokes.punchline: Her comparison of Larry to Marcel Marceau — the silent mime — is meant as a compliment but is actually a devastating insult: she's saying Larry's jokes work despite the words, like a mime
jokes.explanation: The Marcel Marceau line is subtly vicious — she's comparing a talk show host to a mime, meaning his verbal wit is irrelevant. Artie doesn't notice. The layers here are excellent: Angie being accidentally cutting, Artie being oblivious, and the meta-commentary on whether Larry is actually funny. Strong craft.

jokes.text: "Not on TV." — Artie's distinction between having seen the episode in person vs. on television
jokes.setup: Angie points out Artie has already seen the episode he's watching; he says 'many times'
jokes.punchline: His clarification — 'not on TV' — means he's seen it in person (at the taping) but never on Italian television, making the re-watch somehow necessary
jokes.explanation: Three words. 'Not on TV' is Artie at his most magnificently specific — his professional rationale for watching a show he's produced and seen many times is that the Italian broadcast is a new distribution market. The joke works because it's simultaneously insane and completely in-character: Artie's dedication to the show is so total that even a foreign rerun is professionally relevant. One of the episode's strongest moments for character economy.

jokes.text: "What do you want from me? This is my job. I gotta see how it plays in the Italian market."
jokes.setup: Angie challenges why Artie is watching his own show on Italian TV during their romantic vacation
jokes.punchline: Artie invokes professional duty — 'I gotta see how it plays in the Italian market' — as though this is standard industry practice rather than obsession
jokes.explanation: A perfect escalation of the previous joke. 'Not on TV' was the setup; 'the Italian market' is the full justification. Artie has constructed an airtight professional rationalization for watching reruns of his own show while on vacation in Venice. The absurdity is heightened because it's partially plausible — a TV producer might check international broadcasts. Only Artie could say this with a straight face.

jokes.text: Artie and Angie's argument escalates: 'If dressed to kill were on right now, you'd be humping the set crying out "mama mia!"'
jokes.setup: Angie and Artie are fighting about TV vs. romance; Angie calls his show stupid
jokes.punchline: Artie retaliates by imagining Angie equally obsessed with Dressed to Kill — her own Brian De Palma film — with the specific image of her 'humping the set crying mama mia'
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent line. The specificity of 'Dressed to Kill' (Angie Dickinson's famous erotic thriller), the vulgarity of 'humping the set,' and the Italian setting making 'mama mia' land — all working together in one image. It's a perfectly aimed insult that only makes sense in this exact scene with these exact characters. High originality, high character integration.

jokes.text: Artie and Angie's fight escalating — she accuses him of always lashing out, he denies it, then immediately says 'Well, fuck you then'
jokes.setup: Angie says Artie lashes out when she tries to talk to him about his behavior
jokes.punchline: He denies lashing out — 'I don't lash out at you' — and then immediately lashes out: 'Well, fuck you then'
jokes.explanation: This might be the episode's best structural joke. The setup and punchline are one continuous beat — Artie's denial of lashing out IS the lash out, with no gap between them. It's executed in a single breath. The comedy is morally rich: we're laughing at a man who is completely unable to see himself. This is the kind of joke that writers strive for — it's character revelation and comedy simultaneously, with airtight structure.

jokes.text: "Just give me 5 goddamn minutes, then we're gonna take the fucking boat!"
jokes.setup: The Venice argument has been escalating; Angie wants to take the boat and Artie wants to finish watching the show
jokes.punchline: Artie attempts to compromise by offering exactly five minutes before taking the 'fucking boat' — the vulgarity and specificity of the timeframe is the joke
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the juxtaposition: they're in Venice arguing about a boat ride like they're arguing about taking out the trash. The precision of '5 goddamn minutes' and the bathetic 'the fucking boat' reduce the most romantic city in the world to a domestic squabble location. Works well in context.

jokes.text: "Do I look any different? No. Well, I should because I am playing hercules!"
jokes.setup: Hank runs into someone in the hallway
jokes.punchline: He asks if he looks different — the answer is no — and then reveals the reason he should look different: he 'is playing Hercules,' which he has been told literally nothing about yet
jokes.explanation: Hank has already mentally cast himself in the role before Disney has said anything. His certainty that he has transformed — while looking exactly the same — is pure Hank delusion. The setup (do I look different) and punchline (playing Hercules) is structurally clean.

jokes.text: "Hey! They want me! They want me!" — Hank's victorious announcement after the Disney call
jokes.setup: Hank has just gotten a call from Disney
jokes.punchline: His announcement is disproportionately triumphant — and immediately followed by someone's withering slapdown
jokes.explanation: Works primarily as setup for the Dumbo joke that follows. Hank's triumphalism is standard but the repetition of 'they want me, they want me' is Tambor doing physical/vocal comic work that the transcript can't fully capture.

jokes.text: "What are they doing, a live action version of Dumbo? You throw in 40 pounds, a little gray makeup, you're gonna be great."
jokes.setup: Hank announces Disney wants him
jokes.punchline: A colleague immediately imagines Hank as Dumbo the elephant, specifying the weight gain and gray makeup needed
jokes.explanation: A sharp, specific insult. Dumbo is exactly right — it's plausible (large, gray, slightly sad), and the casting breakdown ('40 pounds, a little gray makeup') is delivered as practical advice rather than mockery, which makes it land harder. The joke works because the insult disguises itself as helpfulness.

jokes.text: Hank's Hercules declaration: "I know not this Hank you speak of. As of this day... you shall see only one man. And that man is... HERCULES!"
jokes.setup: Hank has just been insulted; someone calls him 'Hank'
jokes.punchline: He refuses to acknowledge his own name and declares himself to be Hercules, speaking in a theatrical fake-ancient voice
jokes.explanation: Tambor at his finest. The escalation from insulted TV announcer to full Hercules persona is perfect Hank — his ego is so fragile and so vast that it immediately seeks the most grandiose possible refuge. 'I know not this Hank you speak of' is a superb line. The theatrical build to 'HERCULES!' is character comedy of the highest order: only Hank Kingsley would do this.

jokes.text: "I killed my wife, I killed my children, and I shall kill you if you do not temper thy tongue."
jokes.setup: Hank (as Hercules) is threatening the person who insulted him
jokes.punchline: His Hercules threat invokes the actual myth of Hercules killing his own family — which is horrifying context for a workplace threat delivered by a daytime TV announcer
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: it's accurate mythology (Hercules did kill his family as punishment from Hera, which motivated the 12 labors), making Hank accidentally more knowledgeable about Hercules than expected — or he's read this specific detail and missed everything else. The darkness of using familicide as a workplace threat is genuinely funny and shocking. The structure is excellent: the list (wife, children) builds before the threat. Very strong.

jokes.text: "Hank, um, when we said we wanted you to come in for hercules, we meant... hercules the project. Not hercules the role."
jokes.setup: Hank arrives at Disney already in full Hercules mode ('do I look any different?') — he's clearly misunderstood the meeting
jokes.punchline: The exec reveals the brutal miscommunication: they never offered him the title role
jokes.explanation: A beautifully set up and painful deflation. The episode has built Hank's delusion through the audition scene, the hallway declaration, the Hercules persona — and it all collapses in one sentence. 'Hercules the project. Not hercules the role.' is a clean, devastating punchline that the episode has earned.

jokes.text: "I don't mean to question your judgment, but one of my balls is as big as Tate Donovan."
jokes.setup: Hank learns the title role went to Tate Donovan
jokes.punchline: His response — comparing his testicle to Tate Donovan's entire person — is a supremely vulgar expression of contempt
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best lines. The joke earns a 9+ because: it is structurally perfect (the polite opener 'I don't mean to question your judgment, but' followed by the most vulgar possible comparison), it is character-specific (only Hank would say this in exactly this way), it is original (the specific comparison of anatomy to a rival actor's entire body is memorably strange), and the economy is tight (two clauses, zero waste). 'One of my balls' rather than 'both' adds a further comic escalation — as if one is sufficient for the comparison. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: The Hiageus stage direction: '"Hiageus, the village idiot, enters, a sad little stump of a man with a sorry mustache. He's being pelted with stones by a band of toughs. He cries out for hercules in his funny squeal of a voice."'
jokes.setup: The exec describes the role of Hiageus as 'perfect' for Hank
jokes.punchline: The stage directions are read aloud and they are specifically, brutally insulting to Hank's actual appearance and persona — 'sad little stump of a man,' 'sorry mustache,' 'funny squeal of a voice'
jokes.explanation: An exceptionally cruel and precise joke. The stage directions are written as if they describe the Hiageus character in general terms but every detail maps onto Hank Kingsley specifically: the mustache, the stature, the squealing voice, being mocked by a crowd. The exec reads it with enthusiasm as evidence it's a good fit, which makes it even more devastating. The structure — saving the full description until the exec thinks it will sell Hank on the role — is masterful. High rewatch value: you notice more details each time.

jokes.text: He's hercules' partner. He's always getting into all these little scrapes. [pause] And hercules has to... he's the village idiot.
jokes.setup: Hank is being pitched the alternate role of Hiageus
jokes.punchline: The executive's attempt to sell the role — 'little scrapes,' 'partner' — collapses when he accidentally says the quiet part loud: 'he's the village idiot'
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the PR failure — the executive tries to spin the role as something good, then admits 'he's the village idiot' in a moment of exhausted candor. The pause before the admission is likely beautifully played.

jokes.text: "I don't think so." — Hank refusing the Hiageus role after hearing the stage directions
jokes.setup: Hank has just heard a stage description of himself as a 'sad little stump of a man with a sorry mustache' being pelted with rocks
jokes.punchline: Hank's response is a flat 'I don't think so' — the same four words he used when corrected about Samson earlier, now used to reject a description of himself
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'I don't think so' (used earlier to reject correct mythology) gives this an extra dimension. It's now Hank rejecting an accurate description of himself with the same flat confidence he used to reject fact. The economy is perfect — four words does maximum work as both a character beat and a callback punchline. Hank's dignity is completely intact in his own mind; the audience sees everything.

jokes.text: "Are you saying that being the village idiot is my life?"
jokes.setup: The Disney exec has just said the Hiageus role is perfect because Hank is 'living his life'
jokes.punchline: Hank articulates exactly what the exec said — and what the exec frantically tries to walk back
jokes.explanation: The clarifying question IS the joke. Hank naming the subtext — forcing the exec to either confirm or deny that he thinks Hank is a village idiot — is a perfect cringe escalation. The pause after this question must be devastating. Great character moment: Hank has a shred of self-awareness just enough to hear what was said, and we watch it land.

jokes.text: "And Michael eisner thinks hiageus is the best character in the film."
jokes.setup: Hank is rejecting the Hiageus role and walking out; the exec is trying everything to keep him
jokes.punchline: The exec invokes Michael Eisner as the Hiageus enthusiast — which, given the Eisner plane joke earlier, lands as a callback to Hank's desperation to be connected to Eisner
jokes.explanation: The Eisner callback is well-placed — the one thing that might work on Hank is access to the man whose 'air' he claimed to have savored on an airplane. The fact that this is used to sell him on playing the village idiot is perfect irony.

jokes.text: "Do you think that when hiageus gets in trouble, he could say, 'hey, now!'"
jokes.setup: Hank has just rejected the Hiageus role and walked away
jokes.punchline: He turns back to negotiate one condition: that his character gets to say his signature catchphrase — revealing he's already reconsidering and that his price is embarrassingly low
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and a series-level highlight. The structure is perfect: Hank makes a dramatic exit, then immediately returns to negotiate — but his only condition is that the village idiot character gets to say 'hey, now.' This is Hank's entire ego summarized: he will accept humiliation if his brand can survive it. The joke rewards viewers of the whole series (the catchphrase is a running gag across seasons), works structurally (the exit-then-return beat is a classic comic structure), is completely character-specific (no other character could do this), and is economical (the catchphrase in quotes does all the work). The pause after — 'Mmm' from the exec — is the button.

jokes.text: Beverly asks if the new hire worked out — 'How'd that guy turn out?' / 'Ooh, um... good. I still got a job?'
jokes.setup: Artie returns from Venice and Beverly's first question is about a staffing decision he made before leaving
jokes.punchline: Beverly's response to 'good' about the new hire is to immediately check on her own job security
jokes.explanation: A mild workplace comedy beat. Beverly's self-preservation instinct played as casual conversation. Works as scene texture but isn't a standout joke.

jokes.text: "So Larry asked me to move in with him." / "Oh, and are you going to?" / "I don't know. It's too fast. I'm just not sure that I'm ready to... be in a relationship with someone in show business." [pause] "You're in show business." / "Exactly."
jokes.setup: Laura Leighton says she's hesitant about a relationship with someone in show business
jokes.punchline: Beverly points out Laura is herself in show business — and Laura agrees, 'exactly,' as if this confirms her fears rather than invalidates her point
jokes.explanation: A sharp, clean exchange. The structure is perfect: Beverly's observation ('you're in show business') expects to be a contradiction, but Laura accepts it as confirmation of her thesis — she knows exactly what show business does to people because she's in it. The 'exactly' as the punchline is well-calibrated. Insightful showbiz satire compressed into a two-line exchange.

jokes.text: "Boy, I feel like such an idiot. We were on vacation, for Christ's sake. You know, it started out good, but then she wanted to talk about my peccadilloes. My mood swings, my temper, my stubbornness. My obsession with glenlivet. You know the whole fucking laundry list."
jokes.setup: Artie is confiding in Beverly about why the Venice trip collapsed
jokes.punchline: His 'laundry list' of flaws builds from reasonable ones (mood swings, temper, stubbornness) to include his whisky obsession — completing the picture of why relationships with Artie always fail
jokes.explanation: The callback to the Artie/booze metaphor is perfect — he compares Angie to booze early on, and now his problem list includes an 'obsession with Glenlivet.' The word 'peccadilloes' is also funny in this context: it's too polite a word for the list that follows. Strong character integration — this is a full portrait of Artie's self-awareness about his own impossibility as a partner.

jokes.text: So once again I walk alone.
jokes.setup: Artie has just listed all his catastrophic personal failings that ended the Venice trip
jokes.punchline: He concludes with a melodramatic declaration of solitude — 'so once again I walk alone' — as if this is a tragic fate rather than a predictable outcome
jokes.explanation: A classically Artie flourish — grandiose self-pity delivered with total conviction. The solemnity of 'so once again I walk alone' after a list that included 'Glenlivet obsession' is good tonal comedy. Well-delivered absurdist resignation.

jokes.text: Beverly's 'I'm so glad you're back. I'm so glad you're back.' — genuine warmth that undercuts Artie's tragic self-pity
jokes.setup: Artie has declared he walks alone; expects tragic sympathy
jokes.punchline: Beverly's response is practical warmth rather than sympathy — she's glad he's back because he's needed, not because she pities him
jokes.explanation: A functional beat that deflates Artie's melodrama with simple warmth. Not exceptional but lands as a nice tonal counterpoint.

jokes.text: "Oh, shit. I thought she was in London." — Larry on seeing Angie has returned
jokes.setup: Larry and Beverly are in the office when Angie Dickinson apparently arrives
jokes.punchline: Larry's first response to Angie's return is pure alarm — 'Oh, shit' — and his excuse for being unprepared is that he thought she was in London
jokes.explanation: A functional reaction beat but not especially crafted. Works as a comedy of Larry's perpetual unpreparedness.

jokes.text: Artie declaring 'I've got to confront this. I've got to put a stop to it once and for all.' — then going straight to her
jokes.setup: Artie says he must confront Angie and end it permanently
jokes.punchline: The audience knows — and we suspect Artie knows — that 'putting a stop to it' will result in exactly the opposite
jokes.explanation: The situational irony is clear — everything about Artie's character and the episode's pattern guarantees he won't end it. The comedy is in the dramatic sincerity with which he announces his resolve.

jokes.text: Hank introduces his Hiageus voice on Larry's show: 'I'm not playing hercules. They offered me hercules, but I'm playing a much better role. Um, a stretch for me. Uh, the role of hiageus. The village idiot.'
jokes.setup: Hank is being interviewed on Larry's show about his Disney role
jokes.punchline: Hank characterizes the village idiot role as 'a much better role' and 'a stretch' — while calling it by its actual description: 'the village idiot'
jokes.explanation: Hank's spin machine working in full view of an audience that knows better. 'A stretch for me' right before 'the village idiot' is the joke — and Hank saying it with complete sincerity while clearly meaning both. The callback to the whole Disney arc gives it payoff weight.

jokes.text: "You're not... you're not supposed to call it that." — Larry responding to Hank calling it 'the village idiot'
jokes.setup: Hank has just referred to his Disney role as 'the village idiot' on live TV
jokes.punchline: Larry's correction — 'you're not supposed to call it that' — implies there was supposed to be a sanitized version of the description that Hank has abandoned
jokes.explanation: Larry's awareness that there was a PR version of this story — and that Hank has blown it — is a good meta-joke about show management. Works as a tight beat.

jokes.text: "Well, do you want to do a little of the voice? Why don't you do a little of the voice and then we'll be the judge."
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to recover the segment after the 'village idiot' revelation
jokes.punchline: He asks Hank to do the voice, setting up another potential humiliation — and the episode cuts before we hear it, leaving the audience to imagine the worst
jokes.explanation: Works primarily as a structural tease — we don't get to hear Hank's village idiot voice, which may be funnier than hearing it. The cut to commercial is the button.

jokes.text: "'Cause I imagine that must have been very, very difficult." / "It was, but it's cool now. She's on her way to Mexico, and her flight leaves in an hour." / "What time's your flight?" / "9:30." [beat] "I'll be back on Monday."
jokes.setup: Larry asks how Artie's conversation with Angie went; Artie says it went well and she's leaving for Mexico
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Artie is also going to Mexico — to follow Angie again — replays the entire episode's setup in a single exchange
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and thematic button. The whole episode has been about Artie's inability to resist Angie — and the final exchange reveals he's learned nothing. The structure perfectly mirrors the earlier Italy setup ('just 3 days,' 'I'll be back on Monday'). 'What time's your flight?' is the setup; '9:30' is the punchline that doesn't need further explanation. Larry's 'I swear. Thanks, buddy' is the acceptance of the inevitability. It's a satisfying circular ending and works as a series-style runner about Artie's permanent flaw. Very high craft.

tmdb_overview: Artie falls off the wagon with his second addiction, Angie Dickinson, and flies to Venice with her. Larry's affair with Laura Leighton stumbles over their obsessions with watching their own TV shows. Hank auditions for a voice part in the new Disney movie, Hercules.
